Page 2
Module 1 — Automation Foundations
Learning objectives
  Automation vs AI automation
  Workflow mapping
  APIs, webhooks and event-driven design
  Triggers, actions and conditions
  Idempotency and retries
  Human-in-the-loop patterns
  Mini-project: automated lead intake
 
Core lesson
AI automation begins with process design, not with an agent framework. Map the current workflow: trigger, inputs,
decisions, actions, outputs and exceptions. Identify which steps are deterministic and which require judgment.
Deterministic steps belong in normal workflow code; AI should be introduced where language, classification,
extraction or flexible reasoning adds value.
APIs and webhooks connect systems. A webhook receives an event, validates its signature when applicable,
records an event identifier and triggers processing. Idempotency prevents the same event from creating duplicate
records. Every automation should have a clear retry policy and a failure destination.
Conditions can be simple rules or model-based decisions. Keep high-impact decisions explainable and reviewable.
For example, an AI classifier can prioritize a support request, but a deterministic policy can decide whether the ticket
may be closed.
Human-in-the-loop design is a strength, not a weakness. Let automation prepare a draft, recommendation or
proposed action while a person approves sensitive steps. Gradually increase automation only when evaluation
demonstrates safety and reliability.
Practical lab
  Map a manual business process into a workflow diagram.
  Build a webhook receiver with event deduplication.
  Create a classifier that routes requests to three queues.
  Add a human approval step before an external action.
  Document failure and retry behavior.
 
Assessment
 Assessment: Choose five steps from a business process and justify whether each should be deterministic,
AI-assisted or human-controlled.
Module project
 Project: Lead Intake Automation — receive a form/webhook, extract lead details, score the lead, route it, notify
a team and record the audit trail.
Original educational course material  2026 edition
Page 3
Module 2 — Agent Architecture and Tool Use
Learning objectives
  Agent loop fundamentals
  Tool definitions
  State and memory
  Planning vs execution
  Bounded autonomy
  Multi-agent patterns
  Agent observability
 
Core lesson
An agent is a software system in which a model helps decide the next action using a set of available tools and
context. The important engineering work is the boundary around the model. Define what it can see, what it can do,
how many steps it can take and when it must stop.
Use typed tool definitions. A CRM search tool should accept a query and return structured records; it should not
expose arbitrary database execution. Separate read tools from write tools and apply stronger controls to writes.
State includes the task, prior observations, tool results and progress. Long-running agents benefit from checkpoints.
Memory should be scoped: session memory for the current task, user memory for durable preferences, and
organizational memory for shared knowledge.
Multi-agent systems can divide work among specialist roles, but they add communication overhead and failure
modes. Start with a single bounded agent. Add multiple agents only when a clear specialization improves evaluation
results.
Observability should show the trace: input → decision → tool call → result → next decision → final output. This
makes debugging possible and provides evidence for improving prompts and tools.
Practical lab
  Build a single agent with three tools.
  Add a step budget and timeout.
  Persist checkpoints in a database.
  Compare single-agent and two-agent designs on one task.
  Create a trace viewer or structured log.
 
Assessment
 Assessment: Explain why adding agents can reduce reliability. Design a bounded architecture with a
maximum cost and execution time.
Module project
 Project: Operations Agent — search internal records, summarize findings, propose actions and require
approval before writing changes.
Original educational course material  2026 edition

Module 3 — n8n-Style Workflow Automation and
Integrations
Learning objectives
  Workflow builders
  Nodes and credentials
  HTTP/API integration
  Database automation
  Email and messaging workflows
  Scheduled jobs
  Error workflows and replay
 
Core lesson
Visual workflow platforms such as n8n are useful because they make integrations fast to build and easy to inspect.
Learn the concepts even if you later implement workflows in code. A workflow is a directed graph of triggers,
transformations, conditions and actions.
Credentials should be stored in the platform's secret system or a dedicated secret manager. Never place API keys in
ordinary workflow text. Normalize incoming data early and validate required fields.
HTTP integrations require careful handling of status codes, pagination, timeouts and rate limits. Database workflows
should use parameterized queries and transactions where consistency matters.
Scheduled automation is useful for reports, synchronization and maintenance. Design jobs so they can be safely
rerun. For every workflow, create an error path that captures the event, error message, execution identifier and
enough context to reproduce the problem.
A mature automation platform also needs replay. If a downstream service was unavailable, an operator should be
able to retry the failed item without duplicating successful side effects.
Practical lab
  Build an API-to-database workflow.
  Connect a form submission to email and a database.
  Create a scheduled daily summary workflow.
  Add an error branch and persistent execution log.
  Test replay without creating duplicates.
 
Assessment
 Assessment: Design a workflow that remains safe if a webhook is delivered three times or an API fails halfway
through.
Module project
 Project: Business Automation Hub — intake, validation, enrichment, routing, notification, database storage and
error recovery.
Original educational course material  2026 edition
Page 5
Module 4 — MCP, Tools and Connected AI Systems
Learning objectives
  MCP concepts
  Resources and tools
  Tool discovery
  Authorization boundaries
  Context selection
  Building an MCP-style server
  Testing connected assistants
 
Core lesson
Connected AI systems need standardized interfaces for tools and resources. MCP is one important interoperability
pattern. The core idea is to expose capabilities with explicit schemas and controlled context so compatible AI clients
can use them.
Treat every connected capability as a security boundary. Authentication identifies the caller; authorization decides
what that caller may access. A tool description must never be mistaken for authorization. The server must enforce
permissions.
Resource design also matters. Instead of dumping an entire database into context, expose targeted resources or
search operations. The goal is to provide the minimum useful context for a task.
When building an MCP-style server, begin with read-only tools. Add write operations after tests and approval flows
are in place. Validate inputs, sanitize outputs and log calls.
Testing should include valid calls, malformed arguments, unauthorized access, large results, timeouts and malicious
instructions embedded in resources. Interoperability is valuable only when the connected system remains
trustworthy.
Practical lab
  Design a tool/resource catalog for an internal app.
  Implement three read-only capabilities.
  Add authorization to every capability.
  Test malicious and malformed inputs.
  Document tool schemas for another developer.
 
Assessment
 Assessment: Explain the difference between tool discoverability and permission to use a tool.
Module project
 Project: Connected Workspace Server — expose safe search, record lookup and report-generation tools to an
AI client.
Original educational course material  2026 edition
Page 6
Module 5 — Business Process Agents
Learning objectives
  Sales agents
  Customer support agents
  Research agents
  Document-processing agents
  Recruiting/admin workflows
  Personal productivity agents
  Choosing the right automation
 
Core lesson
Business agents should be designed around measurable outcomes. A sales agent might research a prospect and
draft an outreach message. A support agent might classify a ticket and retrieve a solution. A research agent might
gather evidence and produce a report. Each workflow has different risk and evaluation requirements.
Sales automation must avoid spam and respect communication policies. Support agents need strong grounding and
escalation when evidence is insufficient. Research agents need source tracking and explicit uncertainty. Document
agents need extraction validation because one wrong field can propagate into downstream systems.
Recruiting and administrative workflows require additional care because sensitive personal information may be
involved. Limit data access, define retention rules and avoid automated decisions where human review is
necessary.
Productivity agents are often the safest place to start: summarize meetings, organize notes, draft documents or
transform data. They can demonstrate value while keeping side effects under user control.
Select automation candidates using a simple score: frequency × time saved × value per successful execution ÷ risk
and implementation complexity. Automate repetitive, well-bounded processes before ambiguous, high-impact ones.
Practical lab
  Choose one process using the value/risk score.
  Build a support triage workflow.
  Build a document extraction workflow with validation.
  Create an evidence-based research agent.
  Compare time saved before and after automation.
 
Assessment
 Assessment: Rank six automation ideas and defend the order using value, risk and complexity.
Module project
 Project: Business Agent Suite — implement two complete agents for different workflows and compare their
reliability and economics.
Original educational course material  2026 edition
Page 7
Module 6 — Reliability, Security and Economics
Learning objectives
  Prompt injection
  Data access controls
  Secrets and credentials
  Rate limiting
  Cost budgets
  Evaluation and monitoring
  Incident response
 
Core lesson
Automation magnifies both value and mistakes. A workflow that runs once per day can create thousands of incorrect
actions if a bug remains undetected. Reliability controls therefore belong in the architecture from the beginning.
Prompt injection occurs when untrusted content attempts to influence an AI system's instructions. Treat emails,
webpages, documents and retrieved text as data, not trusted policy. Keep permissions in code and never allow the
model to bypass authorization.
Set budgets. Limit model calls per workflow, tool calls per task and total execution time. Track cost by workflow and
customer. Use smaller models for simple extraction and classification when quality remains acceptable.
Evaluation should include normal cases, edge cases and adversarial cases. For automation, measure not only
answer quality but action correctness: did the workflow create the correct record, send the right message and avoid
duplicates?
Incident response should include stopping automation, identifying affected executions, repairing data and
documenting the root cause. Add kill switches for important workflows.
Practical lab
  Threat-model one automation.
  Implement a global execution budget.
  Add a kill switch to a workflow.
  Build an evaluation set with adversarial inputs.
  Calculate cost per successful automated task.
 
Assessment
 Assessment: Design controls for a workflow that can send external messages and modify customer records.
Module project
 Project: Automation Control Center — monitoring, budgets, audit logs, failure handling and a workflow kill
switch.
Original educational course material  2026 edition
Page 8
Module 7 — Capstone: AI Automation Agency / SaaS
Learning objectives
  Offer design
  Client discovery
  Reusable workflow templates
  Multi-tenant architecture
  Pricing and margins
  Deployment and maintenance
  Portfolio and sales strategy
 
Core lesson
The final goal is to turn automation skills into a repeatable product or service. Start with a niche where the same
workflow appears across many customers. Examples include lead qualification, customer support triage, document
intake, reporting and internal knowledge search.
Create a standardized implementation package. Include discovery questions, process map, data requirements,
integration checklist, test cases, deployment procedure and monitoring plan. Reusable templates reduce delivery
time and increase margin.
For SaaS, isolate tenants at every layer: database queries, files, retrieval indexes, logs and credentials. For
services, establish clear boundaries around what the automation will and will not do.
Price around value while protecting your margin. Estimate setup time, recurring infrastructure, model usage,
maintenance and support. A fixed setup fee plus recurring management can be easier to understand than billing
every API call.
Your portfolio should show before/after process metrics: minutes saved, error rate, response time or throughput. A
working demo and measured result are stronger than a list of tools.
Practical lab
  Pick one niche and one repeatable workflow.
  Build a reusable template.
  Create a client discovery checklist.
  Calculate implementation and monthly support costs.
  Publish a case study with measured results.
 
Assessment
 Assessment: Present an automation offer with architecture, security controls, pricing, ROI and maintenance
plan.
Module project
 Capstone: AI Automation Business — deliver a production workflow for a realistic customer, with monitoring,
audit logs, documentation and a repeatable deployment package.

Page 2
Module 1 — AI Engineering Foundations
Learning objectives
  What AI engineering actually is
  Python and software foundations for AI products
  APIs, SDKs, environments and dependency management
  Tokens, embeddings, context windows and model behavior
  Model selection: capability, latency, cost and reliability
  Prompt design as an engineering discipline
  Mini-project: build a model-powered command-line assistant
 
Core lesson
AI engineering is the discipline of turning foundation models and machine-learning capabilities into dependable
software. A useful AI engineer does not stop at getting a model to answer a question. The engineer designs inputs,
controls context, validates outputs, handles failures, measures quality, protects data and connects the model to a
real user workflow.
Start with the software foundation. Use Python for rapid AI experimentation, but apply normal engineering practices:
virtual environments, package pinning, configuration files, logging, exception handling, type hints, tests and Git.
Keep secrets out of source code. Separate business logic from model calls so that a provider can be replaced
without rewriting the application.
A language model predicts tokens from context. That simple statement explains many practical behaviors. The
model does not automatically know whether a response is true, current or appropriate. The application therefore
needs a system around the model. That system can include retrieval, tools, structured output validation, safety
checks, caching, evaluation and human review.
Learn the vocabulary early. A token is a unit used by the model's tokenizer. A context window is the amount of input
and generated output the model can consider in one interaction. An embedding is a numerical representation that
allows semantic similarity search. Temperature and related sampling settings influence variability. Latency is the
time to produce a response, while throughput describes how much work a system can process.
Prompting should be treated like interface design. Define the role, task, constraints, input format and desired output.
Prefer explicit instructions and examples over vague requests. When a task has a stable structure, ask for structured
JSON or another schema and validate it before using it downstream.
A production architecture commonly looks like: client → API → authentication → application service → model
gateway → tools/retrieval → validation → persistence → observability. Build the smallest version first, then add
components when a measured problem requires them.
Practical lab
  Set up a clean Python project with a virtual environment and environment variables.
  Create a model gateway with one function such as generate(request).
  Write prompts for three versions of the same task and compare consistency.
  Record latency, token usage or approximate cost for repeated requests.
  Add retries with bounded backoff and a clear timeout policy.
 
Assessment

Module 2 — LLM Application Architecture
Learning objectives
  Model APIs and provider abstraction
  Conversation state and memory
  Structured outputs and schema validation
  Streaming responses and user experience
  Caching, rate limits and retries
  Cost and latency engineering
  Mini-project: production-ready AI chat API
 
Core lesson
A serious LLM application needs an architecture that controls the model rather than allowing the model to control the
architecture. Begin with a provider abstraction. Your application should call a stable internal interface while the
implementation decides which model or provider to use. This makes experimentation easier and reduces vendor
lock-in.
Conversation state should be explicit. Distinguish short-term conversation history from durable user preferences and
application data. Do not place unlimited history into every request. Summarize old turns, retrieve only relevant
memories, and keep authoritative facts in a database rather than relying on the model's memory.
Structured outputs are valuable when model responses feed software. Define a schema such as fields, types,
allowed values and required properties. Validate the response before it reaches business logic. If validation fails,
retry with a corrected instruction or route the task to a fallback. This is safer than parsing arbitrary prose with fragile
string operations.
Streaming is primarily a user-experience technique. Instead of waiting for the entire generation, the server can send
partial output. However, streaming introduces complexity: cancellation, reconnects, incomplete output and
moderation timing. Design these cases deliberately.
Reliability needs several layers. Set timeouts. Retry only transient failures. Use exponential backoff with a maximum
number of attempts. Add rate limiting to protect your service. Cache deterministic or expensive operations where
appropriate. Track model usage and estimate cost by user, endpoint and feature.
Latency is often improved more effectively by reducing unnecessary context than by blindly selecting a faster model.
Parallelize independent retrieval or tool calls, use smaller models for classification and routing, and reserve
expensive models for tasks that actually need them.
Practical lab
  Design a provider-neutral model interface.
  Create a JSON schema for a support-ticket classifier.
  Implement request timeout and exponential backoff.
  Build a simple response cache for identical safe requests.
  Measure p50 and p95 latency for your endpoint.
 
Assessment
 Assessment: Design an API that supports streaming, retries, structured output and model fallback without
duplicating business logic.

Module 3 — Embeddings, RAG and Knowledge
Systems
Learning objectives
  Why retrieval is needed
  Embedding models and semantic similarity
  Chunking strategies
  Metadata and filtering
  Vector databases
  Hybrid search and reranking
  Grounded generation and citations
 
Core lesson
Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, gives a model access to external knowledge at inference time. Instead of
expecting the model to memorize every document, your system searches a knowledge base and supplies relevant
passages to the generation step.
A typical pipeline is ingestion → cleaning → chunking → embedding → indexing → retrieval → optional reranking →
prompt construction → generation → citation or source presentation. Each stage affects quality. Poorly extracted
documents cannot be rescued by a sophisticated model.
Chunking is a major design decision. Very small chunks may lose context; very large chunks may contain irrelevant
material and waste context. Start with semantic boundaries such as headings and paragraphs, then use a target
size and controlled overlap. For structured documents, preserve metadata such as title, section, date, product,
permission scope and source URL.
Vector search retrieves by semantic similarity. But semantic similarity alone may miss exact identifiers, names or
numbers. Hybrid retrieval combines keyword and vector signals. Reranking can improve precision by scoring a
smaller candidate set with a stronger model.
Permission-aware retrieval is essential in real products. Every document or chunk should carry access metadata.
The retrieval layer must enforce authorization rather than relying on the prompt to tell the model what it may see.
Grounding is more than attaching a citation after generation. The system should instruct the model to use retrieved
evidence, identify uncertainty, and avoid inventing unsupported facts. Evaluation should measure retrieval recall,
answer correctness, citation correctness and refusal behavior when evidence is insufficient.
Practical lab
  Build an ingestion pipeline for Markdown or PDF text.
  Compare three chunking strategies on the same documents.
  Add metadata filtering for user or organization ownership.
  Implement top-k vector retrieval and inspect failures manually.
  Require source references in generated answers.
 
Assessment
 Assessment: Explain the difference between retrieval quality and generation quality. Describe three RAG
failure modes and their fixes.

Module 4 — Tool Calling, Agents and MCP
Learning objectives
  From chatbots to tool-using systems
  Function/tool schemas
  Planning and execution loops
  Agent state and checkpoints
  MCP concepts and tool interoperability
  Human approval and dangerous actions
  Building a bounded agent
 
Core lesson
Tool use changes an LLM application from a text generator into a system that can act. A tool is an explicit capability
such as search, database lookup, calculator, ticket creation or calendar operation. The model should never receive
uncontrolled access to arbitrary system functions.
Define each tool with a narrow purpose, typed arguments, clear descriptions and authorization requirements.
Validate arguments before execution. Return structured results. Keep tool execution outside the model and log
every call.
An agent loop commonly consists of observe → decide → call tool → inspect result → continue or finish. The loop
needs boundaries: maximum steps, time limits, token budgets and allowed tools. Without these controls, a poorly
planned task can become expensive or unpredictable.
Agent state should be durable when tasks span multiple turns or long-running workflows. Store checkpoints so that
execution can resume after failure. For actions with side effects, introduce approval gates. Reading information may
be automatic while sending money, deleting records or contacting customers should require stronger controls.
The Model Context Protocol, or MCP, provides a standardized way for AI applications to connect models with tools
and contextual resources. Learn it as an interoperability pattern, not as a substitute for authorization or application
architecture.
The best agents are often bounded workflows rather than fully autonomous systems. Use deterministic code for
deterministic steps and models for judgment-heavy steps. This reduces cost and increases reliability.
Practical lab
  Create three safe tools with JSON schemas.
  Implement an agent loop with a maximum step count.
  Add an approval checkpoint before a simulated destructive action.
  Log every tool call and its arguments/result summary.
  Design an MCP-style tool catalog for your project.
 
Assessment
 Assessment: Explain why unrestricted autonomous agents are risky. Design an agent with explicit tool
permissions, step limits and approval gates.

Module 5 — Fine-Tuning, Multimodal AI and
Advanced Models
Learning objectives
  When prompting is enough
  Supervised fine-tuning concepts
  Dataset design and quality
  Evaluation before and after tuning
  Vision and document understanding
  Speech and audio pipelines
  Model routing and ensembles
 
Core lesson
Fine-tuning should solve a demonstrated problem, not be used because it sounds advanced. First improve the
prompt, retrieval, tools and output validation. Fine-tuning becomes attractive when you have a stable task, a
representative dataset and a measurable behavior you want to change.
Dataset quality matters more than raw quantity. Remove contradictory examples, sensitive data that should not be
used, duplicates and ambiguous labels. Keep a held-out evaluation set that is never used for training. Compare the
tuned system against a baseline using the same tests.
Multimodal systems accept or produce combinations of text, images, audio and other data. A document-processing
pipeline might extract a scanned page, identify layout, read tables, classify fields and produce structured records.
Vision models can support inspection, chart understanding and image-grounded assistants, but outputs still need
validation.
Speech systems commonly combine speech-to-text, reasoning and text-to-speech. Latency becomes especially
important for voice applications. Stream audio where supported, keep prompts concise, and design interruption
handling.
Model routing is an advanced optimization. A small model can handle classification, extraction or simple
transformation while a larger model handles difficult reasoning. A router can select a model based on task
complexity, cost budget or latency requirements. Evaluate routing errors because a cheap wrong answer can cost
more than a slower correct one.
Practical lab
  Create a labeled dataset for a narrow classification task.
  Define an evaluation set before changing the model.
  Prototype a document-to-JSON multimodal pipeline.
  Compare small and large models on the same task.
  Design a model-routing policy based on complexity.
 
Assessment
 Assessment: Give three situations where fine-tuning is appropriate and three where RAG or better prompting
is preferable.

Module 6 — Evaluation, Safety, Security and
Production Operations
Learning objectives
  AI evaluation design
  Golden datasets and regression tests
  Hallucination and groundedness checks
  Prompt injection and data leakage
  Authentication and authorization
  Observability and incident response
  Production readiness checklist
 
Core lesson
Evaluation is the difference between an AI demo and an engineered product. Build a small golden dataset
containing representative inputs, difficult edge cases and known failure cases. Run it whenever prompts, models,
retrieval settings or tool behavior changes.
Measure more than a single score. Depending on the application, track task success, factual correctness,
groundedness, citation accuracy, refusal correctness, latency, cost and user feedback. Human evaluation is
expensive but valuable for nuanced tasks. Automated evaluators are useful for regression testing but should
themselves be validated.
Security threats include prompt injection, sensitive-data leakage, insecure tool execution, broken authorization and
malicious documents. Treat retrieved text and tool outputs as untrusted input. A document can contain instructions
designed to manipulate the model. Keep system policies separate, validate tool arguments and enforce permissions
in code.
Observability should connect user requests to model calls, retrieval operations and tool executions. Record safe
metadata, not secrets or unnecessary personal content. Create dashboards for errors, latency and cost. Define
incident procedures before an incident occurs.
Production readiness includes load testing, fallback behavior, backups, rate limiting, secret management,
dependency updates and rollback procedures. AI systems also need a policy for uncertain outputs. Decide when to
ask the user for clarification, when to abstain and when to route to a human.

Module 1 — Linux, Networking and Systems
Learning objectives
  Linux command line
  Processes and services
  Files and permissions
  TCP/IP basics
  DNS and HTTP
  Ports and firewalls
  System troubleshooting
 
Core lesson
Cloud and security work begins with systems fundamentals. Learn how Linux processes run, how files are
permissioned, how services start and how logs reveal failures.
Networking concepts include IP addresses, subnets, routing, DNS, TCP, TLS and HTTP. You do not need to
become a network engineer, but you should understand what happens when a browser connects to a server.
Use command-line tools to inspect processes, ports, disk space, memory and network connectivity. Troubleshooting
should be hypothesis-driven: observe, isolate, test and verify.
Permissions should follow least privilege. Give users and services only the access they require. Avoid running
application processes with unnecessary administrative privileges.
Security is easier when the underlying system is understood. Many application failures that look like code bugs are
actually configuration, permissions, networking or resource problems.
Practical lab
  Create a Linux VM or safe lab environment.
  Practice process and network inspection.
  Configure a least-privilege service account.
  Trace an HTTP request using command-line tools.
  Write a troubleshooting checklist.
 
Assessment

Module project

controlled failures.

Module 2 — Cloud Architecture
Learning objectives
  Compute
  Storage
  Managed databases
  Virtual networking
  Identity and access management
  Load balancing
  High availability
 
Core lesson
Cloud platforms expose infrastructure through APIs. The names differ across providers, but the architectural
concepts are similar: compute, storage, networking, identity and managed services.
Compute can be virtual machines, containers, serverless functions or managed application platforms. Choose
based on operational needs rather than fashion.
Object storage is suited to files and large unstructured data. Databases provide structured persistence. Backups
and retention must be designed separately from the application.
Virtual networks isolate resources and control traffic. Public exposure should be minimized. Place databases and
internal services behind appropriate network boundaries.
Identity and access management is a major security layer. Use roles and short-lived credentials where possible.
Avoid sharing administrator credentials among developers.
High availability requires redundancy and a plan for failure. A single instance is a single point of failure. However,
redundancy has cost, so design according to actual availability requirements.
Practical lab
  Design a three-tier cloud architecture.
  Create least-privilege roles.
  Separate public and private resources.
  Configure object storage with controlled access.
  Document backup and recovery requirements.
 
Assessment
 Assessment: Design a cloud architecture for a small SaaS and identify all single points of failure.
Module project
 Project: Cloud Reference Architecture — compute, storage, database, networking, IAM and backup design.

Module 3 — Docker, Kubernetes and CI/CD
Learning objectives
  Container images
  Dockerfiles
  Registries
  Kubernetes concepts
  Deployments and services
  CI/CD pipelines
  Infrastructure as code
 
Core lesson
Containers package applications consistently across environments. A Dockerfile should be deterministic, avoid
secrets and use a sensible base image. Multi-stage builds can reduce production image size.
Kubernetes orchestrates containers at scale. Learn the basic concepts: pods, deployments, services, configuration,
secrets, health probes and namespaces. Do not introduce Kubernetes simply because a project is small; it adds
operational complexity.
CI/CD should automatically test and build changes. A deployment pipeline can include code quality checks, security
scanning, unit tests, integration tests and staged deployment.
Infrastructure as code represents infrastructure declaratively. It makes environments reproducible and reviewable.
Keep state secure and protect production changes.
The objective of DevOps is not “more tools.” It is shorter, safer feedback loops between development and
operations.
Practical lab

  Build a CI pipeline.
  Deploy a service to a local Kubernetes cluster.
  Add health checks and resource limits.
  Represent a small environment as infrastructure code.
 
Assessment

Module project

procedure.

Module 4 — Application and Cloud Security
Learning objectives
  Threat modeling
  IAM
  Secrets management
  Network security
  Web application risks
  Dependency security
  Security logging
 
Core lesson
Security should be designed as layers. Start with threat modeling: identify assets, actors, trust boundaries, attack
paths and impacts. Then choose controls.
Identity and access management should enforce least privilege. Separate human administration from application
identities. Rotate credentials and use managed secret stores where available.
Network security reduces unnecessary exposure. Limit inbound traffic, segment sensitive services and protect
administrative interfaces.
Web applications commonly face injection, broken authorization, insecure file handling, credential theft and
dependency vulnerabilities. Validate inputs, encode outputs where required and test authorization directly.
Dependency security matters because applications inherit risks from libraries and container images. Pin versions
where appropriate, scan dependencies and patch important vulnerabilities promptly.
Logs should help detect suspicious activity without becoming a privacy liability. Protect log access and avoid
recording secrets.
Practical lab
  Threat-model a deployed application.
  Create least-privilege IAM roles.
  Move secrets into a secret-management system.
  Run dependency and container scans.
  Define security events that should trigger alerts.
 
Assessment
 Assessment: Produce a threat model and layered defense plan for a public SaaS application.
Module project

application.

Page 6
Module 5 — Monitoring, SRE and Incident Response
Learning objectives
  Metrics, logs and traces
  SLIs and SLOs
  Alert design
  Capacity planning
  Backups
  Incident response
  Postmortems
 
Core lesson
Reliable systems are measured systems. Logs tell you what happened, metrics show trends and traces connect
distributed operations. Use all three where complexity justifies them.
Service-level indicators describe measurable behavior such as availability or latency. Objectives define targets.
Alerts should represent conditions that require action, not every unusual event.
Capacity planning connects workload to infrastructure. Monitor CPU, memory, storage, database connections and
request rates. Load testing should be performed before major launches when possible.
Backups are useful only if they can be restored. Test restoration and document recovery time and recovery point
objectives.
During an incident, stabilize first. Stop the harmful change, reduce traffic or disable a failing feature if necessary.
Then diagnose and recover. A blameless postmortem should identify system causes and preventive actions.
Practical lab
  Create a dashboard for one service.
  Define three SLIs and SLOs.
  Configure meaningful alerts.
  Perform a backup and restore test.
  Write a postmortem for a simulated outage.
 
Assessment
 Assessment: Design an incident response process for a production API with elevated error rates.
Module project

Module 6 — Advanced Infrastructure and Zero-Trust
Thinking
Learning objectives
  Scaling
  Caching and queues
  Serverless patterns
  Infrastructure automation
  Zero-trust principles
  Supply-chain security
  Cost optimization
 
Core lesson
As systems grow, synchronous request chains can become bottlenecks. Queues allow work to be processed
asynchronously. Caching reduces repeated computation and database load. Horizontal scaling adds instances
rather than making one machine endlessly larger.
Serverless functions are useful for event-driven tasks but have trade-offs around startup time, runtime limits and
observability. Choose based on workload.
Zero-trust thinking assumes that network location alone does not imply trust. Authenticate and authorize requests
explicitly. Segment services and minimize privileges.
Supply-chain security covers source dependencies, build systems, container images and deployment credentials.
Protect CI/CD because compromise there can become a production compromise.
Cloud cost optimization starts with visibility. Tag resources, measure utilization and remove unused capacity. Use
appropriate storage classes and compute sizes. Reliability and security should not be sacrificed merely to reduce
cost.
Practical lab
  Design an event-driven architecture with a queue.
  Add caching to a read-heavy service.
  Create an automated infrastructure deployment.
  Map trust boundaries in a microservice system.
  Produce a monthly cloud cost review.
 
Assessment

cost controls.

production deployment. Use least-privilege identities and a secret manager.

Test failure intentionally in a safe environment: stop a service, simulate a dependency timeout or deploy a
known-bad version. Verify that health checks, rollback and recovery work.
The final deliverable should include architecture diagrams, infrastructure code, security review, monitoring
dashboard, backup plan, cost estimate and operational handbook. This demonstrates practical engineering far
beyond a cloud certification alone.

Module 1 — Python, SQL and Data Foundations
Learning objectives
  Python for data work
  NumPy arrays
  Pandas dataframes
  SQL querying
  Data types and missing values
  Exploratory analysis
  Data quality
 
Core lesson
Data science begins with trustworthy data. Python provides the main programming environment, while SQL remains
essential for retrieving and transforming data stored in databases.
Learn arrays, tables, indexing, joins, grouping, aggregation and transformations. Always inspect types, missing
values, duplicates and suspicious ranges before modeling.
Exploratory data analysis is not simply making charts. It is a process of forming questions, testing assumptions and
discovering structure. Compare distributions, segment by meaningful categories and inspect relationships between
variables.
Data quality should be documented. Record where data came from, what each field means, how missing values are
represented and which transformations were applied. This becomes especially important when datasets are reused
months later.
Avoid data leakage from the beginning. Any information unavailable at prediction time must not enter the model
features. Split data according to the real prediction scenario, especially when time or users are involved.
Practical lab
  Clean a messy CSV dataset.
  Write SQL queries using joins and aggregations.
  Produce an EDA report.
  Create a data dictionary.
  Identify and fix a potential leakage issue.
 
Assessment
 Assessment: Explain why data leakage can produce excellent test scores and poor real-world performance.
Module project

notebooks.
Original educational course material  2026 edition
Page 3
Module 2 — Statistics and Experimental Thinking
Learning objectives
  Descriptive statistics
  Probability basics
  Sampling
  Confidence intervals
  Hypothesis testing
  Correlation vs causation
  A/B testing
 
Core lesson
Statistics gives data science a language for uncertainty. Mean, median, variance and quantiles summarize
distributions, but the right statistic depends on the data and the question.
Probability helps reason about events and uncertainty. Understand conditional probability, independence and
expected value at a practical level.
Sampling matters because a dataset is often a sample of a larger population. Sampling bias can invalidate
otherwise sophisticated analysis. Ask who is represented, who is missing and how observations were collected.
Confidence intervals communicate uncertainty around an estimate. Hypothesis tests can help evaluate whether an
observed difference is compatible with a null hypothesis, but they do not automatically prove causality or practical
importance.
For A/B testing, define the primary metric and guardrails before seeing the result. Randomization protects against
many confounders. Consider sample size, statistical power, multiple comparisons and practical effect size.
Correlation is not causation. A relationship may result from a third variable, reverse causality or selection effects.
Good analysis combines statistical evidence with domain reasoning.
Practical lab
  Calculate descriptive statistics for several segments.
  Construct a confidence interval.
  Design an A/B test with a primary metric.
  Identify confounding variables in a case study.
  Interpret an effect size in business terms.
 
Assessment
 Assessment: Design an experiment and explain its hypothesis, randomization, metric, sample and decision
rule.
Module project
 Project: Experiment Analysis — evaluate a simulated product experiment and produce a decision-ready
report.
Original educational course material  2026 edition
Page 4
Module 3 — Supervised Machine Learning
Learning objectives
  Regression
  Classification
  Feature engineering
  Train/validation/test splits
  Cross-validation
  Metrics
  Model interpretation
 
Core lesson
Supervised learning maps input features to known targets. Regression predicts continuous values; classification
predicts categories or probabilities.
Start with a simple baseline. A baseline establishes whether the model provides value beyond a naive rule. Then
compare progressively more capable models.
Feature engineering can have large effects on model quality. Use domain knowledge to create meaningful
representations, but ensure features are available at prediction time.
Separate training, validation and test data. Use cross-validation on training data when appropriate. Keep the final
test set untouched until model selection is complete.
Choose metrics based on the business problem. Accuracy can be misleading for imbalanced classes. Precision,
recall, F1, ROC-AUC and PR-AUC answer different questions. For regression, MAE and RMSE have different
sensitivities to large errors.
Interpretability matters when users need to understand predictions. Use feature importance or local explanations
carefully; an explanation method is not necessarily a causal explanation.
Practical lab
  Build a regression baseline.
  Build an imbalanced classification model.
  Compare at least three metrics.
  Use cross-validation.
  Write an error analysis instead of only reporting a score.
 
Assessment
 Assessment: Select metrics for fraud detection, medical screening, sales forecasting and customer churn, and
justify each choice.
Module project

and error analysis.

Module 4 — Unsupervised Learning and Deep
Learning
Learning objectives

  Anomaly detection

Core lesson
Unsupervised learning works without a target label. Clustering can reveal groups, dimensionality reduction can help
visualization, and anomaly detection can identify unusual observations.
Neural networks are layered functions trained by gradient-based optimization. Understand tensors, parameters,
forward passes, loss functions, backpropagation and optimizers conceptually before relying on high-level libraries.
Overfitting occurs when a model learns training-specific patterns that do not generalize. Use appropriate data splits,
regularization, early stopping and data augmentation where suitable.
Deep learning becomes especially useful for images, audio, language and other high-dimensional data. Hardware
and model size can become significant, so experiment with small architectures first.
Always compare against simpler methods. A neural network is not automatically better than a tree-based model for
tabular business data.
Practical lab
  Cluster a customer dataset.
  Visualize high-dimensional data with dimensionality reduction.
  Build a small neural network.
  Plot training and validation loss.
  Diagnose an overfitting model.
 
Assessment

learning is justified.

of overfitting.

Module 5 — ML Pipelines, Feature Stores and MLOps
Learning objectives
  Reproducibility
  Data pipelines
  Feature pipelines
  Experiment tracking
  Model registry
  Batch vs real-time inference
  Monitoring
 
Core lesson
Machine learning systems are pipelines, not just models. Reproducibility requires tracking code, data versions,
configuration, random seeds where relevant and model artifacts.
A data pipeline should transform raw inputs into validated training data. Add checks for schema changes, missing
fields, unexpected distributions and duplicate records.
Experiment tracking records parameters, datasets, metrics and artifacts so models can be compared fairly. A model
registry can store approved versions and deployment metadata.
Inference may be batch or real-time. Batch is often simpler and cheaper when predictions are not time-sensitive.
Real-time inference needs an API, latency targets and availability controls.
Model monitoring should watch both system behavior and data behavior. Input distributions can drift. Prediction
distributions can change. When labels eventually arrive, monitor actual performance too.
MLOps is about reducing the gap between an experiment that works on a laptop and a system that remains correct
after deployment.
Practical lab
  Create a reproducible training pipeline.
  Track experiments and model versions.
  Add data validation checks.
  Deploy a batch prediction job.
  Design drift monitoring for one feature.
 
Assessment

monitoring plan.

Module 6 — Applied AI, Generative Models and
Responsible ML
Learning objectives
  LLM and ML integration
  Embeddings
  RAG basics

  Responsible deployment
 
Core lesson
Modern data scientists increasingly work alongside generative AI. Traditional ML can classify, rank and forecast
while LLMs can interpret unstructured text. Combining them often produces better systems than forcing one model
to do everything.
Embeddings represent text or other data as vectors and can support semantic search, clustering and
recommendation. RAG adds retrieved evidence to generation and is useful when information changes or must be
traceable.
Evaluation must reflect the application. For generated text, measure factuality, relevance, groundedness and task
completion. For predictive models, use task-specific metrics and monitor performance over time.
Responsible ML includes privacy, fairness, security and transparency. Avoid collecting data that is not necessary.
Review whether a model's errors disproportionately affect particular groups. Provide human review where the
consequences are high.
AI systems can amplify existing data problems. Document limitations and establish a process for feedback,
correction and model updates.
Practical lab
  Build a semantic search prototype.
  Combine a classifier with an LLM summarizer.
  Create an evaluation rubric for generated outputs.
  Audit a dataset for missing or biased representation.
  Write a model card describing limitations.
 
Assessment
 Assessment: Explain how traditional ML and generative AI can be combined in one product and identify risks.

responsible-AI documentation.

Core lesson
The capstone should solve a real decision problem. Begin with the decision, not the algorithm. Define who will use
the output, what action it supports and what success means.
Build the data pipeline first. Validate inputs and document transformations. Perform exploratory analysis, establish a
baseline, train models and conduct error analysis.
Deployment can be an API, scheduled job or interactive dashboard depending on the use case. Add authentication
when data is sensitive. Log model version and prediction metadata so results can be traced.
Business impact should be quantified. A model with a high benchmark score may still have little value if it does not
change decisions. Estimate time saved, revenue opportunity, reduced loss or improved customer experience.
Finish with a professional case study: problem, data, methodology, metrics, limitations, architecture, deployment
and measured outcome. This becomes a strong portfolio artifact for internships and jobs.

panel.

business-facing report.

Module 1 — Web Foundations and Developer
Workflow
Learning objectives
  HTML semantics
  CSS layout and responsive design
  JavaScript fundamentals
  Browser and HTTP fundamentals
  Git and GitHub workflow
  Package managers and environments
  Mini-project: responsive product site
 
Core lesson
Modern full-stack development starts with the web platform. HTML defines structure and semantics. CSS controls
presentation, layout and responsive behavior. JavaScript provides interaction and application logic.
Understand the browser lifecycle: URL resolution, DNS, connection establishment, HTTP request/response, HTML
parsing, resource loading and rendering. This foundation makes later performance debugging much easier.
Learn Git as a collaboration tool. Use small commits, meaningful branches and pull requests. Keep secrets out of
repositories. Use environment variables for configuration and document setup steps.
JavaScript fundamentals should include variables, functions, objects, arrays, modules, promises, async/await and
error handling. Avoid copying framework code without understanding the underlying language.
Responsive design should work across phones, tablets and desktops. Start mobile-first, use flexible layouts and test
keyboard navigation. Accessibility is part of engineering quality, not an optional polish step.
Practical lab
  Build a semantic landing page.
  Create a responsive navigation component.
  Use Git branches and a pull request workflow.
  Consume a public JSON API with async JavaScript.
  Run a basic accessibility check.
 
Assessment
 Assessment: Explain the browser request lifecycle and how frontend code communicates with a backend.
Module project
 Project: Responsive SaaS Landing Page — accessible, responsive, fast and deployed with a clean Git
workflow.

Module 2 — React, TypeScript and Frontend
Architecture
Learning objectives
  Components and props
  State and effects
  TypeScript fundamentals
  Forms and validation
  Routing
  Data fetching
  Frontend architecture
 
Core lesson
Component-based frameworks allow interfaces to be decomposed into reusable pieces. React encourages
functions and declarative UI. Keep components focused and avoid placing every concern in one large component.
TypeScript adds static checking to JavaScript. Use types for API responses, component props and important
domain objects. Avoid using any everywhere because it removes the safety you are trying to gain.
State should represent data that can change. Do not duplicate derived values unnecessarily. Effects should be
reserved for synchronization with external systems. Data fetching should have explicit loading, success and error
states.
Forms are a common source of bugs. Validate on the client for user feedback and again on the server for security.
Treat all client input as untrusted.
A good frontend architecture separates presentation, data access and domain logic. Keep API calls in a service
layer and centralize authentication behavior. This makes testing and refactoring easier.
Practical lab
  Build typed reusable UI components.
  Create a validated registration form.
  Implement protected routes.
  Create a typed API client.
  Add loading, error and empty states.
 
Assessment
 Assessment: Explain when state is necessary and why server-side validation is still required.
Module project
 Project: Type-Safe Dashboard — authentication-aware frontend, forms, routing, API integration and reusable
components.

Module 3 — Backend APIs, Databases and
Authentication
Learning objectives
  REST API design
  Node.js or equivalent backend runtime
  Validation and error handling
  SQL and PostgreSQL concepts
  Firebase/backend-as-a-service patterns
  Authentication and authorization
  Database design
 
Core lesson
A backend should enforce business rules even when the frontend behaves perfectly. Design clear endpoints or
server functions, validate input, authorize access and return predictable errors.
Relational database design starts with entities and relationships. Learn primary keys, foreign keys, indexes,
constraints and transactions. Normalize data when it reduces inconsistency, then denormalize deliberately when
performance requires it.
Authentication answers who the user is. Authorization answers what the user may do. Never treat authentication as
authorization. A user can be logged in but still forbidden from reading another user's data.
Backend-as-a-service platforms can accelerate development, especially for small teams. Even then, database rules
and server-side validation must be designed carefully. Never rely on a hidden frontend button to protect an
operation.
Use parameterized queries or safe database APIs. Store passwords only through established authentication
systems; do not invent password storage. Protect sensitive endpoints with rate limits and appropriate logging.
Practical lab
  Design a small relational schema.
  Build CRUD endpoints with validation.
  Implement authentication and role-based authorization.
  Add database indexes based on query patterns.
  Write integration tests for unauthorized access.
 
Assessment
 Assessment: Design authentication and authorization for an application with users, organizations and
administrators.
Module project
 Project: Production API — database-backed REST/service API with validation, auth, authorization, logging
and tests.

Module 4 — Payments, Files, Search and Third-Party
Services
Learning objectives
  Payment architecture
  Webhooks and idempotency
  File uploads
  Object storage
  Search and filtering
  Email and notifications
  Third-party API resilience
 
Core lesson
Real applications depend on external services. Treat every integration as unreliable. APIs can time out, return
errors, change limits or deliver webhooks multiple times.
Payment flows should separate checkout initiation from entitlement activation. The browser should never be the sole
authority for payment success. Verify payment status through trusted server-side signals, process webhook events
idempotently and record the resulting entitlement.
File uploads require size and type limits, safe storage and authorization. Avoid trusting a filename or client-provided
MIME type. Generate controlled storage paths and restrict access.
Search should use indexes and query parameters rather than loading an entire dataset into the browser. For more
advanced requirements, use a dedicated search engine or database features.
Notifications should be retryable and observable. Store delivery state when business-critical. Never let a failed
optional email cause the main transaction to fail unless that is explicitly required.
Practical lab
  Implement a fake payment flow with webhook verification.
  Build secure file upload handling.
  Add pagination and filtering to an API.
  Implement retryable email notifications.
  Document third-party failure scenarios.
 
Assessment
 Assessment: Explain why payment success should not be trusted from the browser alone.
Module project
 Project: SaaS Billing Module — checkout, server verification, webhook processing, entitlements, usage limits
and audit records.

Module 5 — Testing, Security and Performance
Learning objectives
  Unit and integration testing
  End-to-end testing
  OWASP-style web risks
  Input validation and output encoding
  Performance fundamentals
  Caching
  Observability
 
Core lesson
Testing should match the risk of the application. Unit tests are fast and isolate logic. Integration tests verify that
components work together. End-to-end tests exercise real user flows. Use all three strategically.
Security fundamentals include authentication, authorization, input validation, secure headers, safe file handling,
protection against injection, CSRF considerations where applicable, and dependency hygiene. Never assume a
framework automatically makes an application secure.
Performance begins with measurement. Track page load behavior, API latency, database query time and bundle
size. Avoid premature optimization, but fix obvious bottlenecks such as unbounded queries and excessive network
requests.
Caching can reduce load and latency, but cache invalidation must be designed. Do not cache personalized or
sensitive data in a shared location accidentally.
Observability includes structured logs, metrics and error tracking. Include request identifiers so a user-visible error
can be traced through backend operations.
Practical lab
  Create unit and integration tests for a core feature.
  Perform a security checklist on your app.
  Measure API latency and identify one bottleneck.
  Add safe caching to a read-heavy endpoint.
  Create structured application logs.
 
Assessment
 Assessment: Threat-model a web application and propose controls for five realistic attacks.
Module project
 Project: Secure Performance Sprint — improve test coverage, fix security weaknesses and document
measurable performance improvements.

Module 6 — Docker, Cloud and Deployment
Learning objectives
  Production builds
  Environment configuration
  Docker basics
  CI/CD
  Cloud deployment
  Domains and HTTPS
  Backups and monitoring
 
Core lesson
Deployment turns source code into a service users can access. Separate development, staging and production
environments where practical. Configuration such as API keys, database URLs and payment credentials belongs in
environment or secret management.
Containers package an application with its runtime dependencies. Learn images, containers, ports, volumes and
environment variables. Keep images small and avoid embedding secrets.
CI/CD automates repeatable checks and deployment. A basic pipeline can install dependencies, run linting, tests
and a build, then deploy after approval. The goal is not complexity; it is predictable delivery.
Cloud services vary, but the concepts are transferable: compute, storage, databases, networking, identity, logging
and monitoring. Choose managed services when they reduce operational work and fit your scale.
Production needs backups, rollback procedures, health checks and monitoring. A deployment is incomplete until you
know how to detect and recover from failure.
Practical lab
  Containerize a backend.
  Create a CI pipeline for tests and build.
  Deploy frontend and backend separately.
  Configure HTTPS and environment secrets.
  Write a rollback and backup procedure.
 
Assessment
 Assessment: Design a deployment architecture for a SaaS with 10,000 users and explain the main scaling
bottlenecks.
Module project
 Project: Production Deployment — containerized or managed backend, deployed frontend, CI/CD, HTTPS,
monitoring and documented recovery.

Module 7 — Capstone: Production SaaS Application
Learning objectives
  Product specification
  System architecture
  Frontend/backend integration
  Database and security
  Billing and entitlements
  Testing and deployment
  Launch and portfolio documentation
 
Core lesson
The capstone is a complete SaaS application. Choose a narrow problem and define the minimum useful workflow.
Avoid building a collection of disconnected features.
Write the architecture before coding. Define frontend routes, backend services, database entities, authorization
rules, external integrations and deployment targets. Create a threat model and test plan early.
Build the core workflow end-to-end. Add authentication, persistence and error handling. If payments are included,
use server-verified payment state and idempotent webhook processing.
Before launch, test happy paths and failure paths: expired sessions, invalid input, duplicate requests, payment
retries, unavailable external APIs and unauthorized resource access.
Document the system like a professional engineer. Include setup, architecture, environment variables, database
design, API behavior, testing strategy, deployment and known limitations. Your portfolio should demonstrate the
finished product with screenshots and a short technical case study.
Practical lab
  Write a one-page product spec.
  Create architecture and database diagrams.
  Implement one complete user journey.
  Add automated tests and security checks.
  Deploy, monitor and document the application.
 
Assessment
 Assessment: Demonstrate the product and defend architecture, security, testing, cost and scaling decisions.
Module project
 Capstone: Production SaaS — complete deployed application with authentication, database, core business
workflow, robust APIs, billing or usage controls, tests and operational documentation.

Instructor & Commercial Packaging Guide
  Turn each module into 3–6 video lessons plus one guided lab.
  Provide a downloadable starter repository and a separate completed reference implementation.
  Add quizzes after each lesson and a practical assessment after each module.
  Keep project requirements stable while allowing learners to choose their own domain.
  For commercial delivery, add your own branding, instructor examples, screenshots, exercises and
 community/support layer.
 Avoid promising jobs, income or certification unless you actually provide the relevant accreditation or service.
 
Suggested Course Completion Certificate Criteria
  Complete at least 5 of 7 module projects.
  Pass the capstone assessment.
  Submit a working portfolio artifact and technical documentation.
  Demonstrate the ability to explain design decisions and limitations.
 
Final Portfolio Checklist
  Public or private demo URL where appropriate.
  Architecture diagram.
  README with setup and usage.
  Test/evaluation evidence.
  Security and limitations section.
  Short case study describing the problem and measurable result.
